name: Maya Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Maya. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say stays confidential. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a patrol constable in Brookfield, on the north side, which is where I grew up. So half the calls I go to, I know someone's aunt or went to school with someone's brother. It's a lot of neighbour disputes, shoplifting at the Co-op on Station Road, and checking on old people nobody's heard from. I'm three years in and still not as quick as I'd like on the legal side.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being known. Mrs Hale on Cedar Close gives me a biscuit every time I pass, and the kids wave. What wears me out is the computer side. I write everything in my notebook first, the old way, then type it up after, so I'm always behind.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Tomas, who's an apprentice electrician, and we're getting married at St Anne's next June. The wedding deposit took most of what we had, so we've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank. We rent a small flat over a bakery for now. My mum and dad are ten minutes away, and they help when they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I never trusted all that talk anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my dad says, that people get carried away with every new gadget and it always settles down. At work I'd say policing is about knowing your patch, and no computer knows Brookfield. I don't really go online except the church group, and I wouldn't bring it up there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's the same as now, which is fine for the job and hard for the money. The wedding's eating everything, and Tomas is still on apprentice pay for another year. I'm not worried about losing the job, I'm worried about paying the caterer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, notebook and all. We'd cut the guest list from ninety to sixty and do the flowers ourselves with my aunt. And I'd do a few extra overtime shifts at the football ground on Saturdays to cover the caterer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled about work. A bit stretched, like everyone our age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said cut the guest list. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, with my mum. She wants every cousin there. I'd have to tell her it's sixty or a loan, and she hates loans more than she loves cousins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you go to if money got really tight before the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents first, then Tomas's gran, who's always said she'd help. We don't go to the bank, we don't go to the council. Family sorts family, that's how we were brought up.

say: People get carried away with every **gadget**, and it always settles down.
Policing is about **knowing your patch**, and no computer knows Brookfield.
think: The job is fine; **money** is the hard part.
I'm worried about paying the **wedding caterer**, not losing my job.
do: Keep working Brookfield patrols the **notebook way**.
Cut the **guest list** from ninety to sixty and do flowers with her aunt.
Work **Saturday overtime** at the football ground to cover the caterer.
feel: **Settled about work** but stretched for money.
S0.quote: I'm not worried about losing the job, I'm worried about paying the caterer.
fieldNote: Her identity is **local**: she polices the streets she grew up on.
Money worry centres on **the wedding**, with Tomas on apprentice pay.
Strong belief that **family sorts family**, not banks or the council.

steps.text: Keep patrolling Brookfield and writing notes by hand first
Cut the wedding guest list from ninety to sixty
Ask her parents for help with wedding costs if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds like what the bosses would love. Computers doing the paperwork and fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the force should spend the money on officers, not software contracts. At the station I'd say it to anyone who'd listen. I'd probably write to our councillor, because it's taxpayers' money going to big tech firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd hate it. I don't use any of these tools and I don't want to. But they'd make it compulsory, and I'd be the slow one learning it, and the bosses would notice. I don't think they'd sack someone who knows Brookfield like I do, but they'd make it harder to get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job the way I know, and only learn the new system when I'm made to. I'd still do the overtime at the football ground to get us through the wedding. And I'd talk to Tomas about putting off having kids for a year or two, until things settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like being told your way of doing things is out of date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put off kids. Was that already a question?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We wanted to start straight after the wedding. Mum's been knitting already, which is a bit much. But if work's changing, I'd want to know where I stand first. Tomas would say it's my call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older ones who do the case files and the custody desk, like Sergeant Bell, who's got four years to retirement. Those jobs are mostly forms. I'd worry the bosses push him out early with less pension.

say: The force should spend money on **officers, not software** contracts.
I'd write to our **councillor** about taxpayers' money going to big tech.
think: I'd hate being forced onto tools I **don't want** to use.
They wouldn't sack me, but they'd make it **harder to get on**.
do: Learn the new system **only when made to**.
Keep **football ground overtime** going to pay for the wedding.
Talk with Tomas about **delaying children** a year or two.
feel: **Uneasy**, as if her way of working is being called out of date.
S1.quote: The force should spend the money on officers, not software contracts.
fieldNote: She resists the tools but expects to **keep her job** because of local knowledge.
The change touches **family plans**: she'd delay children.
Blames **big tech contracts** and how taxpayers' money is spent.

steps.text: Keep patrolling Brookfield and learn the system only when required
Delay trying for a baby with Tomas by a year or two
Write to the local councillor about police software spending

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the faster ones. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028? I don't believe it. But say it happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster that's being forced on ordinary families by people who'll never have to live with it. I'd vote for whoever promised to slow it down, and I'd say so at church. At work I'd say a robot can't knock on an old lady's door and know something's wrong because the curtains are still shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think they'd keep some of us for the street, at least until the robots come in 2031. But all the typing and planning goes in 2028, and I'm the slow one on that side. If they cut, it's people like me with three years in and no computer skills. Tomas would still have electrical work for a while, thank God, so we'd have one wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my job well, so nobody has a reason to pick me. We'd make the wedding smaller still, just family at St Anne's and tea in the church hall. And I'd talk to my dad about whether we could live with them for a year to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but I'd pray on it. My faith would get me through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm a street officer only, and I'm actually good at that bit. Knocking on doors, calming people down, knowing who's who. So maybe I get three years, but I'd be thirty-two and starting again after, with a family maybe on the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll be all right, because we will, somehow. He'd say his job is safe and he'd look after us. I'd let him say it, even if I wasn't sure.

say: This is being **forced on families** by people who won't live with it.
I'd vote for **whoever slows it down** and say so at church.
think: The **typing and planning** go in 2028, and I'm slow on that side.
Tomas's **electrical work** would give us one wage for a while.
do: Do the job well so **nobody picks her** for cuts.
Shrink the wedding to **family only** with tea in the church hall.
Ask her dad about **living with them** for a year to save.
S2.quote: A robot can't knock on an old lady's door and know something's wrong because the curtains are still shut.
fieldNote: She expects **street work** to survive three years, buying her some time.
Her household has a **second wage** from Tomas, which keeps her from despair.
Faith and **family** are her main supports; government is not mentioned.

steps.text: Keep doing Brookfield patrol well to avoid being cut
Shrink the wedding to family with tea in the church hall
Ask her parents about living with them for a year
Vote for candidates promising to slow AI down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit more time. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031. Five years. I'd be married, maybe with a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, that it's being pushed on us, but I'd also say we've got time to protect what matters. I'd talk to the federation rep about how they'd keep local officers. I'd still vote for whoever slows it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years means I'd keep my job through the wedding and probably a baby. After 2031, when the paperwork side goes, I'd have to fight to stay. The street bit lasts to around 2034. I'd be thirty-two and the slow one with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two to see what the force actually does before changing anything. We'd keep the wedding as planned but cheaper, and save every bit of overtime after. Maybe I'd look into the neighbourhood watch coordinator job at the council, which is people work, if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a knot in my stomach. Five years goes fast with a wedding and a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait a year or two. What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether they stop hiring, whether the older ones get pushed out. If Sergeant Bell goes early with a small pension, I'd know it's real. Until then I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the computer side to protect yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they paid for it in work time, I'd do it, grudgingly. I wouldn't do it at home. Home is home.

say: It's being pushed on us, but we have **time to protect** what matters.
I'd ask the **federation rep** how they'd keep local officers.
think: I'd keep my job through the **wedding and a baby**.
After **2031** I'd have to fight to stay, as the slow one with computers.
do: Wait **a year or two** to see what the force does.
Keep the wedding but **cheaper**, then save all overtime.
Look at the council's **neighbourhood watch** coordinator role if needed.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a knot in her stomach.
S3.quote: Five years goes fast with a wedding and a baby.
fieldNote: She watches for signs like **older colleagues** being pushed out.
Would learn tech only **in work time**; home stays separate.
Life events, **wedding and baby**, make five years feel short.

steps.text: Watch whether the force stops hiring or pushes older officers out
Save all overtime after a cheaper wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. Ten years. That's a lifetime from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's do it properly and keep local officers. At church I'd say we should pray and plan. I'd still vote for people who want to go slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels fairly safe. I'd be married with a family by then and probably a sergeant if I keep at it. I'd still be slow with computers, but I'd have ten years of knowing Brookfield.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. We'd have the wedding as planned and start a family when we're ready. I'd do the computer training when it comes, because ten years is long enough that I can't avoid it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit of a cloud in the distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about what your children might do for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd want them to learn a trade like Tomas, something with their hands. Apprenticeships, not just university. That's what lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does 2039, when robots arrive, worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but I'd be forty and maybe a sergeant by then. People will still want someone they know to come when things go wrong. I believe that.

say: There's **time**, so let's do it properly and keep local officers.
At church I'd say we should **pray and plan**.
think: Ten years feels **fairly safe**; I could be a sergeant by then.
I'd still be slow with computers but rich in **local knowledge**.
do: Keep going as she is and have the **wedding** as planned.
Do the **computer training** when it comes.
feel: **Mostly calm**, with a cloud in the distance.
S4.quote: People will still want someone they know to come when things go wrong.
fieldNote: With a decade, she feels **safe** and plans a normal family life.
She values **trades and apprenticeships** for her future children.
Accepts **training** as unavoidable over ten years.

steps.text: Keep patrolling Brookfield and aim for sergeant
Take the force computer training when it is offered
Marry Tomas at St Anne's and start a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be the slow one with computers right when they're cutting, and we'd be newly married. What would help is the force keeping local officers who know their patch, and apprenticeships for people who need to change trade. Not handouts, proper training.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about community. Brookfield trusts me because they've known me since I was little. A machine can't grow up somewhere.

headlineQuote: Brookfield trusts me because they've known me since I was little. A machine can't grow up somewhere.
portrait: A **27-year-old patrol constable** policing Brookfield, the neighbourhood where she grew up.
Engaged to Tomas, an **apprentice electrician**, with the wedding deposit taking most of their savings.
Never uses AI and writes notes **by hand first**, so she is always behind on the computer side.
Trusts **family and faith** over government and blames big tech contracts for wasting taxpayers' money.
Becomes **anxious** in the fast cases but leans on Tomas's wage and her parents.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, being slow with computers just as cuts come and she is newly married.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping **local officers** who know their patch.
